title: Frequent Urination: Why Am I Peeing So Much All of a Sudden?
summary: Peeing a lot all of a sudden? Learn what counts as frequent urination, the causes from infection to high blood sugar, and which urine test tells them apart.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Peeing more often than usual often just follows drinking more fluid, caffeine or alcohol. When it starts suddenly and keeps going, the common medical causes are a urinary tract infection (UTI), high blood sugar from diabetes, an overactive bladder and, in middle-aged and older men, an enlarged prostate** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \]. Less often, it comes from diabetes insipidus, a high blood calcium level, kidney disease or a water pill (diuretic) \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \].


A urinalysis is the first test that separates these. Glucose in the urine points to high blood sugar, leukocyte esterase and nitrite point to infection, and a very low specific gravity shows urine that is unusually dilute \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Blood tests then confirm the cause: fasting glucose and HbA1c for diabetes, and a metabolic panel for calcium, sodium and kidney function.


## What counts as frequent urination


**Frequent urination means needing to urinate more often than usual. Urgent urination is a sudden, strong need to go that is hard to delay** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. Needing to go eight or more times a day, or two or more times at night, is one of the ways overactive bladder is described \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/overactivebladder.html) \]. Most people can sleep six to eight hours without having to urinate \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \].


There is no single normal number of trips, because it depends on how much you drink. What matters most is a change from your own usual pattern, especially one that started suddenly and is not explained by more fluid.


### Frequency vs volume


**Peeing often and peeing a lot are two different problems.** Frequency is how many times you go. Volume is how much urine your body makes in a day. MedlinePlus defines an excessive volume, called polyuria, as more than 2.5 liters (about 85 fluid ounces) of urine per day in an adult, and notes that this is different from needing to urinate often \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \].


The difference narrows the cause:


- **Large amounts each time, often with thirst:** the body is making more urine. High blood sugar, diabetes insipidus, drinking a lot of water, high or low blood calcium, kidney disease, diuretic medicines, alcohol and caffeine are the listed causes \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \].
- **Small amounts, often, with urgency:** the body is not necessarily making more urine. Infection, an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate and irritation of the urethra fit this pattern \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \].


A voiding diary helps tell them apart. MedlinePlus suggests writing down when you urinate and how much, along with what you drink, and bringing that record to your visit \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \].


## Everyday causes: fluids, caffeine, alcohol and cold


**Drinking more fluid means making more urine. Among the listed causes of frequent urination, caffeine is a common one and alcohol a less common one** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. Both alcohol and caffeine can also increase the total amount of urine you make \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \]. Drinking a lot in the evening, or having caffeine or alcohol with or after dinner, can cause you to get up at night to urinate \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \].


Cold can trigger the urge too. The NIDDK lists being in a cold environment, such as reaching into a freezer, along with drinking or touching water or hearing running water, as triggers for a sudden, strong urge to urinate \[[6](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/bladder-control-problems/symptoms-causes) \].


If cutting back on fluids late in the day, caffeine and alcohol brings your pattern back to normal, a medical cause is less likely. Frequency that continues when you are not drinking large amounts of fluid is a reason to see a provider \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \].


## Urinary tract infection


**A UTI is one of the most common causes of frequent or urgent urination** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. A bladder infection typically causes a strong need to urinate often, even right after the bladder has been emptied, together with pain or burning when you urinate, pressure or cramping in the lower belly or back, and cloudy or bloody urine that may smell strong \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].


Women get UTIs more often than men because the urethra is shorter and closer to the anus \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. Diabetes, problems emptying the bladder completely, an enlarged prostate and kidney stones also raise the risk \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].


A urinalysis looks for white blood cells, red blood cells, bacteria and nitrites, and can diagnose an infection most of the time. A urine culture identifies the bacteria and helps choose the antibiotic \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. For how to read a positive nitrite result, see[nitrites in urine](https://mitohealth.com/blog/nitrites-in-urine) , and for cloudy urine with these symptoms, see[cloudy urine](https://mitohealth.com/blog/cloudy-urine) .


## High blood sugar and diabetes, with excessive thirst


**Increased urination and feeling very thirsty are two of the most common symptoms of diabetes** \[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \]. When blood glucose is high enough, the kidneys can no longer hold it back and glucose spills into the urine. On a urinalysis, glucose usually appears once blood glucose rises above about 180 to 200 mg/dL \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].


Other common diabetes symptoms include feeling very hungry even after eating, blurred vision, fatigue, sores that do not heal and frequent infections, including UTIs \[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \]. How quickly they appear depends on the type:


- **Type 1 diabetes:** symptoms usually develop quickly, over a few days or weeks, and can include unexplained weight loss \[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \].
- **Type 2 diabetes:** symptoms can develop slowly over several years, and many people have none or do not notice them \[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \].


### Excessive thirst (polydipsia)


**Excessive thirst is an abnormal feeling of always needing to drink fluids, and it can be a symptom of high blood sugar from diabetes that is not controlled** \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]. It is often just a reaction to fluid lost during exercise or to a salty meal \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]. Thirst that is ongoing and unexplained, or that comes with blurry vision or fatigue, is a reason to see a provider \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \]. The tests a provider may order for it include blood glucose, serum calcium, serum sodium and a urinalysis \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003085.htm) \].


For what a glucose result on your urine report means, see[urine glucose](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-glucose) .


## Diabetes insipidus


**Diabetes insipidus is an uncommon condition in which the kidneys cannot concentrate urine, so the body makes a large amount of dilute urine** \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]. It is not the same as diabetes mellitus. Both cause constant thirst and frequent urination when untreated, but in diabetes insipidus blood sugar is normal \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \].


Its symptoms include intense thirst, often with a craving for ice water, a large urine volume, needing to urinate often throughout the day and night, and very pale, dilute urine \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]. It happens either when the brain does not release enough antidiuretic hormone (ADH) or when the kidneys do not respond to it. A high blood calcium level and kidney disease are among the causes of the kidney form \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]. Testing includes blood sodium and osmolality, urine concentration and urine output, and a provider may refer you to an endocrinologist \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \].


## Overactive bladder


**Overactive bladder is a condition in which the bladder squeezes urine out at the wrong time** \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/overactivebladder.html) \]. MedlinePlus describes it as having two or more of these symptoms: urinating eight or more times a day or two or more times at night, a sudden strong need to urinate immediately, or leaking urine after a sudden strong urge \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/overactivebladder.html) \].


Nerve problems, too much fluid or too much caffeine can cause it, and often the cause is unknown \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/overactivebladder.html) \]. Because infection and poorly controlled diabetes cause the same frequency and urgency, a urinalysis and urine culture are among the first tests a provider uses to rule them out \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \].


## Enlarged prostate in men


**An enlarged prostate is a common cause of frequent urination in middle-aged and older men** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. Also called benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), it is not cancer and does not raise the risk of prostate cancer \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \]. The prostate surrounds the urethra, so as it grows it can press on the flow of urine \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \].


Symptoms can include needing to urinate two or more times a night, a strong and sudden urge, a slow or delayed start, a weak stream, straining, dribbling at the end, and the feeling that the bladder has not fully emptied \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \]. Fewer than half of men with BPH have symptoms \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \]. The workup can include a urinalysis and urine culture to check for blood or infection, BUN and creatinine blood tests for kidney function, and a PSA blood test \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \].


## High blood calcium


**A high blood calcium level (hypercalcemia) can cause increased thirst and more frequent urination because of changes in the kidneys** \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. It is most often found on routine blood tests, and most people have no symptoms \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. When symptoms appear, they can also include nausea, constipation, muscle weakness, tiredness or confusion, and bone pain \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \].


The most common cause is an overactive parathyroid gland \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000365.htm) \]. Calcium is part of a basic or comprehensive metabolic panel. For the full symptom list, see[symptoms of high calcium](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-calcium) , and for the reference page on the marker, see[calcium](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/calcium) .


## Diuretic medicines


**Diuretics, often called water pills, are a recognized cause of frequent urination and of a larger urine volume** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \]. Diuretics can also cause nighttime urination. If a diuretic is the cause, a provider may suggest taking it earlier in the day \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \]. Other medicines can affect urination too, so bring a full medicine list to any visit about urinary symptoms \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \].


## Frequent urination at night


**Needing to get up at night to urinate is called nocturia. Normally the body makes less urine at night, which lets most people sleep six to eight hours without going** \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \].


The common causes are drinking a lot of fluid, caffeine or alcohol before bed, a bladder or urinary tract infection, and an enlarged prostate \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \]. Other causes include diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, leg swelling, a high blood calcium level, diuretics and diabetes insipidus \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \]. Waking often to urinate can also be linked to obstructive sleep apnea and other sleep disorders \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \].


Contact a provider if waking to urinate continues over several days, the number of trips bothers you, or it comes with burning or blood in your urine \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003141.htm) \].


## Frequent urination in women and men


**Women and men share most causes of frequent urination: fluids, caffeine, infection, high blood sugar and an overactive bladder. A few causes belong to one sex** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \].


**In women,** UTIs are more common because the urethra is shorter and closer to the anus. Sexual activity, using a diaphragm and menopause all raise the risk \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. Vaginitis, swelling of or discharge from the vulva and vagina, is another common cause of frequent or urgent urination \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. Pregnancy also causes frequent urination \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. Discharge from the vagina along with urinary symptoms is a reason to contact a provider \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \].


**In men,** an enlarged prostate is the leading sex-specific cause, especially from middle age on \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \]. Infection or inflammation of the prostate (prostatitis) can also cause painful, frequent urination, and it raises PSA too \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/prostate-specific-antigen-psa-test/) \]. Discharge from the penis along with urinary symptoms is a reason to contact a provider \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \].


## Frequent urination on a urinalysis


**A urinalysis separates the causes of frequent urination by reading several lines together: glucose, ketones, leukocyte esterase, nitrite, blood and specific gravity, plus white and red blood cells from the microscopic exam** \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. No single line explains frequency on its own. The pattern does.


Report line What it adds for frequent urination


[Glucose](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-glucose) Usually appears once blood glucose rises above about 180 to 200 mg/dL. Often a sign of uncontrolled diabetes \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Ketones](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-ketones) Not normally found in urine. Can come from diabetic ketoacidosis, low food intake or a ketogenic diet \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Leukocyte esterase](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-leukocytes) An enzyme from white blood cells. Positive with inflammation and infection \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Nitrite](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-nitrite) Made by many bacteria. More specific for infection than leukocyte esterase, but a negative result does not rule a UTI out \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Blood](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/occult-blood) Detects red blood cells, but free hemoglobin and muscle protein can also make it positive. The microscopic exam confirms bleeding \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Specific gravity](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-specific-gravity) How concentrated the urine is. Near 1.010 suggests normal hydration. Below 1.003 suggests very dilute urine \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


### Why a negative nitrite can mislead when you pee often


**Bacteria need about four hours in the bladder to turn nitrate into nitrite, so false-negative nitrite results are common when someone is urinating frequently** \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. That matters here, because frequent urination is exactly the symptom being investigated. Some bacteria, such as Enterococcus, do not make nitrite at all \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].


A negative nitrite with a positive leukocyte esterase, white blood cells or bacteria under the microscope, and burning when you urinate can still be an infection. That is where a urine culture helps \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].


### Reading the lines together


- **Glucose positive, ketones negative:** points to high blood sugar. Fasting glucose and HbA1c are the next step \[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]\[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \].
- **Glucose and ketones both positive, with thirst, nausea or fatigue:** possible diabetic ketoacidosis. This needs prompt care \[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
- **Leukocyte esterase or nitrite positive, white cells or bacteria seen:** a likely urinary infection. A culture identifies the bacteria \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
- **Everything negative, specific gravity below 1.003, with large volumes and thirst:** very dilute urine. That fits drinking a lot of water, diabetes insipidus or kidneys that cannot concentrate urine. A metabolic panel with sodium, calcium and kidney function is the next step \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \]\[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \]\[[4](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
- **Everything negative, specific gravity normal, small amounts often:** infection and sugar are less likely. Bladder and prostate causes do not show on a urinalysis, so a provider looks at how the bladder fills and empties instead \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \].
- **Blood positive with red blood cells seen:** bleeding somewhere in the urinary tract. Bloody urine with frequency is a reason to see a provider \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]. For how to read the result, see[blood in urine test results](https://mitohealth.com/blog/blood-in-urine-test-results) .

## Which blood tests come next


**The urinalysis points the way, and blood tests confirm the cause. The three that matter most for frequent urination are fasting glucose with HbA1c, a metabolic panel, and, for men with prostate symptoms, PSA** \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000381.htm) \]\[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \].


### Fasting glucose and HbA1c for diabetes


A fasting[glucose](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/glucose) shows blood sugar at one moment. An[HbA1c](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hba1c) test shows the average blood glucose over the past two to three months, and it is used to screen for and diagnose type 2 diabetes and prediabetes \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]. Urinating a lot and feeling very thirsty are among the symptoms MedlinePlus lists as reasons for the test \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]. Blood glucose tests have largely replaced the urine glucose test for diagnosing and monitoring diabetes, so a positive urine glucose is a reason to check blood sugar, not a diagnosis on its own \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003581.htm) \].


Mito offers a[glucose test](https://mitohealth.com/products/glucose) and an[HbA1c test](https://mitohealth.com/products/hemoglobin-a1c-with-reflex-to-1-5-anhydroglucitol-1-5-ag) . For how the two work together, see[testing for diabetes: the two key blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/testing-for-diabetes-the-two-key-blood-tests-you-should-know) .


### A metabolic panel for calcium, sodium and kidney function


**A basic metabolic panel (BMP) measures glucose, calcium, sodium, potassium, carbon dioxide, chloride, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine, which together reflect fluid balance and how well the kidneys are working** \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/basic-metabolic-panel-bmp/) \]. Those are the blood tests MedlinePlus lists for an excessive urine volume: blood sugar, BUN, creatinine and electrolytes \[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \].


Each marker answers a different question.[Calcium](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/calcium) checks for hypercalcemia.[Sodium](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/sodium) helps evaluate water balance, including in diabetes insipidus \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000377.htm) \].[Creatinine](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/creatinine) and[eGFR](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/egfrcr) show kidney filtering. Most people with early chronic kidney disease have no symptoms, and blood and urine tests are often the only way to find it \[[17](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/chronic-kidney-disease-ckd/what-is-chronic-kidney-disease) \].


Mito offers a[basic metabolic panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/basic-metabolic-panel-bmp) and a[comprehensive metabolic panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp) , which adds liver and protein markers. For what each result means, see[metabolic panel explained](https://mitohealth.com/blog/metabolic-panel-explained-what-your-blood-test-means) and[kidney disease symptoms and blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/kidney-disease-symptoms-and-blood-tests) .


### PSA for men: a discussion with a clinician


**A prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test can be part of the workup when a man has frequent, slow or painful urination** \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/prostate-specific-antigen-psa-test/) \]. It is not a test for an enlarged prostate on its own. A high PSA can come from an enlarged prostate, prostatitis, a urinary tract infection, certain medicines or prostate cancer, and the test cannot show which \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/prostate-specific-antigen-psa-test/) \].


Using PSA to screen for prostate cancer has possible benefits and harms, so MedlinePlus advises deciding together with your provider based on your risk, general health and preferences \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/prostate-specific-antigen-psa-test/) \]. A UTI can raise PSA \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/prostate-specific-antigen-psa-test/) \], so a result from during an infection can be hard to read. Mito offers a[PSA test with reflex to free PSA](https://mitohealth.com/products/psa-total-with-reflex-to-psa-free) . For more on the marker, see[PSA: what it means for men](https://mitohealth.com/blog/prostate-specific-antigen-men-cancer-healthy) and[symptoms of high PSA](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-psa) .


## When to get prompt care for frequent urination


**Contact a provider right away if frequent urination comes with fever, back or side pain, vomiting or shaking chills. These can be signs that an infection has reached the kidneys** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. A kidney infection can also cause a fever above 101°F (38.3°C), and in older people, mental changes or confusion are sometimes the only signs of a UTI \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].


**Also get care right away for:**


- increased thirst or appetite, fatigue or sudden weight loss together with frequent urination \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \];
- fruity-smelling breath, trouble breathing, belly pain, nausea or vomiting with high blood sugar, which can be diabetic ketoacidosis, a medical emergency \[[8](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/symptoms-causes) \];
- being unable to pass urine or empty your bladder \[[6](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/bladder-control-problems/symptoms-causes) \];
- blood in your urine \[[6](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/bladder-control-problems/symptoms-causes) \].


**See a provider soon** if you urinate often or urgently and are not drinking large amounts of fluid, if you pass a large amount of urine over several days without an explanation, if you have cloudy urine, or if the symptoms have changed how you live or you are leaking urine \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003140.htm) \]\[[2](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003146.htm) \].

## Frequently asked questions


### Should I be worried if I am peeing a lot?


Usually not, if it follows more fluid, coffee, tea or alcohol and settles once those do. MedlinePlus advises contacting a provider if you urinate often or urgently but are not pregnant and are not drinking large amounts of fluid, if you pass a large amount of urine over several days without an explanation, or if you have bloody or cloudy urine. Contact a provider right away if peeing a lot comes with fever, back or side pain, vomiting or shaking chills, or with more thirst or appetite, fatigue or sudden weight loss.


### Does peeing a lot mean my kidneys are working well?


No. How much you pee mostly reflects how much you drink. It is not a measure of kidney function. Kidney disease can itself increase urine volume or nighttime urination, and early chronic kidney disease usually causes no symptoms at all. Kidney function is measured with blood and urine tests, such as creatinine and eGFR in a metabolic panel and protein on a urinalysis.


### Is it normal to pee every 30 minutes?


Not as an everyday pattern. It can happen for a short while after a lot of fluid, coffee or alcohol. Needing to go eight or more times a day, or two or more times at night, is how overactive bladder symptoms are described, and frequent urination that keeps going without extra fluid is a reason to see a provider. Very frequent peeing with burning or pain points toward a urinary infection, and passing large amounts with intense thirst points toward high blood sugar or, less often, diabetes insipidus.


### Why do I keep peeing after I just peed?


A strong need to urinate often, even right after the bladder has been emptied, is a classic bladder infection symptom, especially with burning, pressure low in the belly, or cloudy or strong-smelling urine. In men, an enlarged prostate can leave the bladder not fully emptied, with dribbling at the end of urinating. An overactive bladder can also cause sudden urges soon after you go. A urinalysis is the first test to check for infection.
